title: Seven verses, said seventeen times a day
hook: the Fatiha is recited in every unit of every prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, the whole book, this year's khatm, and your line: from the opening, onward. Did you choose a reading time, and did it hold? Day three hundred thirty-three.

Do some arithmetic with a Muslim who prays all five daily prayers. Dawn has two units of prayer, called rak'ahs. Noon has four. Afternoon, four. Sunset, three. Night, four. Add them up: seventeen. And in every one of those seventeen units, standing, the same short surah is recited. Seventeen times a day, before any optional prayers are counted. Over a year, more than six thousand times, from the same seven verses. Today: seven verses.
screen: `TWO, FOUR, FOUR, THREE, FOUR.` → `SEVENTEEN UNITS A DAY.` → `THE SAME SURAH IN EACH.`

segments.voice: Last year you learned al-Fatiha a line at a time. This year we stand back and look at the whole surah, and at what happens to words when they're repeated. The rule comes from a hadith in Bukhari and Muslim: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said there is no prayer for the one who does not recite the Opening of the Book. So the Fatiha is the one surah that can't be left out. Schools of law differ on one detail. Many say every worshipper recites it in each unit. Hanafi scholars teach that when you pray behind an imam, you stand silent, and the imam's recitation counts for the whole row. Either way, it's said in every unit. The Qur'an itself seems to point to this. In Surah al-Hijr, God tells the Prophet He has given him seven of the oft-repeated verses, and the great Qur'an. Many commentators, following a hadith in Bukhari, say those seven are the Fatiha. Its Arabic nickname comes from there: as-sab' al-mathani, the seven oft-repeated. In the count printed in many copies today, the bismillah is the first of the seven; some scholars count differently and still arrive at seven. Now the question repetition raises. Doesn't anything said seventeen times a day go numb? Muslim teachers raise it themselves. Scholars warn against prayer that's only motion, and teachers tell students to slow down, to hear one line freshly each time. The repetition is the container. What's poured into it changes from one prayer to the next. The most repeated words, said by a tired person at dawn and a grieving one at night, are never quite said the same way twice.
screen: `NO PRAYER WITHOUT THE OPENING` · `THE SEVEN OFT-REPEATED (15:87)` · `DOESN'T REPETITION GO NUMB?` · `THE SAME WORDS, NEVER SAID THE SAME`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count how many times you say it today. If you pray, keep a quiet tally, a finger pressed against your thumb after each unit, and notice which time was most awake. If you don't pray, count something else: how many times today you hear the opening line, Praise be to Allah, or say it in your head. Right now, say the seven verses once, slowly, aloud or silently, or just sit with the number seventeen. The bell holds the time.
Seven verses. Al-Fatiha, the seven oft-repeated, recited in every unit of every prayer: seventeen times a day in the obligatory prayers alone. Today's word.
Your line: the most repeated words. Today, pick one of the seventeen, or one moment if you don't pray, and say it as if for the first time. Day three hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims recite al-Fatiha standing in every rak'ah of every prayer, seventeen times a day across the five obligatory prayers; in the Hanafi school a worshipper praying behind an imam listens silently while the imam recites.

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory: Bukhari 756 and Muslim 394 (no prayer without the Fatiha); Bukhari 4474 (Fatiha as the seven oft-repeated). Please confirm.
Rak'ah counts (2, 4, 4, 3, 4 = 17) are the obligatory units; Shia practice also has seventeen, though prayers are often combined into three times. Confirm the phrasing 'a Muslim who prays all five'.

Recitation behind the imam: stated as 'many say every worshipper recites it; Hanafi scholars teach silence behind the imam.' Maliki and Hanbali positions distinguish loud and silent prayers; confirm the simplification is fair.
Verse count: the Kufan count (used in the Hafs mushaf) includes the bismillah as 1:1; others count it differently and split verse 7. Confirm.
'Over a year, more than six thousand times' is 17 x 365 = 6,205; confirm the arithmetic is acceptable.
